Summary

Five speaking lessons (L2 to L6), one a week from the week of 16 November to the week of 14 December 2026. They follow the diagnostic lesson (L1). The students chose the focus: tenses (past especially), sentence structure, and little words like still, already and yet. The unit starts from simple sentence order in the present. It moves to the past simple (regular, then irregular and questions), then still, already and yet. It ends with a short spoken interview about their own past and recent life. Four threads run every lesson: a timed "Talk for a minute" that gets longer each week, a grammar page in the notebook, a growing little words bank, and an error tracker of their own mistakes.

55-minute lesson rhythm

Every lesson follows the same 55-minute rhythm, so students always know what comes next.

Part Min Mode
1. Fix the errors (from last lesson's tracker) 5 Say it, then write
2. The rule: one stepped example 8 Say it
3. Drill: say it fast (picture or prompt cards) 10 Say it
4. Game (different each lesson) 10 Say it
5. Talk for a minute (ladder) 10 Say it
6. Notebook: rule box and little words 7 Write
7. Exit ticket: three sentences 5 Write
← Unit at a glanceLesson threads →

Threads that run every lesson

  • Talk for a minute ladder: one timed talk per lesson on a picture prompt. L2 45 s, L3 60 s, L4 75 s, L5 90 s, L6 90 s in the final task. Each talk must use the newest grammar point.
  • Grammar page: one rule box per lesson copied into the notebook, with three model sentences. By L6 the notebook holds the whole spine as revision.
  • Little words bank: a back page of the notebook. Each lesson adds 4 to 6 words with one example sentence.
  • My errors tracker: the teacher notes 2 or 3 real errors per student during speaking. They start the next lesson as "Fix the errors" (anonymised) and students copy the fixed version.
← 55-minute rhythmGrammar spine →

Grammar spine

  1. L2: English word order (who + does + what + where + when). Present simple statements, negatives and questions.
  2. L3: Past simple of regular verbs (-ed), the three -ed sounds, was/were.
  3. L4: Top 15 irregular verbs. Past questions and negatives with did.
  4. L5: still, already, yet, just as fixed chunks with the present perfect ("I've already eaten", "I haven't finished yet"). Contrast with the past simple: finished time = past simple.
  5. L6: Everything together in the interview.

Verb bank (built over L3 and L4)

L6 interview questions (types shown from L2, exact questions used in the L4 mini mock and L6)

  1. What do you usually do at the weekend?
  2. What did you do last weekend?
  3. Where did you go? Who did you go with?
  4. Did you like it? Why or why not?
  5. What did you eat yesterday?
  6. Have you finished your homework for this week yet?
  7. Is there something you still want to do this year?
  8. Talk for 1 minute: A day I remember (picture prompts: a birthday, a trip, a match, a holiday).

Levels per strand

Strand Not yet Partly Achieved
Past tense Uses the present for past events Some correct past forms, errors with irregulars or did Mostly correct past simple, including did questions and negatives
Sentence order French word order, missing subject or verb Correct in short sentences, slips in longer ones Correct order with time and place at the end
Little words None or wrong place Uses 1 or 2 correctly Uses 3 or more correctly, including one of still, already, yet
Fluency One-word answers, long pauses Short sentences, needs prompts Keeps going 60 to 90 s with linking words
← Interview questionsCommon errors →

Traps for French speakers to rehearse

  • "I have 15 years" for I am 15. "I am agree" for I agree.
  • "I like very much football": adverb between verb and object.
  • "Yesterday I go": present after a past time word.
  • "I didn't went", "Did you saw?": double past.
  • "I have seen him yesterday": present perfect with a finished time (passé composé transfer).
  • "Already" at the end of the sentence, "yet" in positive sentences.
  • -ed pronounced as an extra syllable everywhere ("play-ed").
← Assessment levelsTeacher notes →

Key design decisions and teacher notes

  • Sentence order first, before tenses. At weak A1, past forms collapse without a stable sentence frame. L2 gives them the frame that every later tense slots into.
  • Past simple only, split over two lessons. Regular verbs and was/were (L3) before irregular verbs and did (L4), so each lesson has one new idea.
  • still, already, yet taught as chunks, not as the present perfect. Full present perfect is beyond weak A1. Students learn three or four fixed patterns they can say with confidence. Pushed to L5 because the chunks need the past participle, which overlaps with the irregular verbs from L4.
  • Mini mock in L4, error clinic in L5. Students hear the final task format a fortnight before, and L5 fixes what the mock showed.
  • Speaking first, writing small. Each lesson has one notebook panel and a short exit ticket. The notebook becomes their revision for L6.
  • Attendance is uneven (2 of 4 at L1). Every lesson starts from the notebook rule box and the errors tracker, so an absent student can catch up in 5 minutes. L6 has a 10-minute buffer for a catch-up interview.
  • Pairs or trios: all games work with 2 to 4. With 2, the teacher plays the third role.
  • Assumptions: one 55-minute lesson a week, starting the week of 16 November, ending before the Christmas break. All French L1. No school-wide rubric, so the four strands are this unit's own.

Open decisions

  1. Day and frequency: is it one lesson a week, and which day? Do the dates run to the week of 14 December?
  2. Final task: is the L6 interview useful as is, or do the students' main teachers need something specific (oral exam prep for the brevet, for example)?
  3. Reporting: do the levels go anywhere (main English teacher, parents), or are they only for the students?
  4. The two absent students: will they join from L2? If so, a 5-minute catch-up on the L1 diagnostic at the start of L2.
